15:27: Just as in 15:25, Paul speaks as if Christ will one day stand on or rest his feet on the enemies. In Paul’s culture, kings or generals might stand on or put their feet on leaders that they conquered. This showed that these leaders were conquered and had to submit to the king or general who conquered them.

Here, {it is} clear indicates that someone is pointing out something that is or should be obvious. In other words, the author does not need to argue for what is clear and can instead just point it out.
Here the Corinthians would have known that the one having put everything is God the Father.
Here, excepted identifies something as an “exception” to a general rule or statement. Here Paul means that the one having put everything is not included in everything.
15:28: Paul here refers to God the Son as opposed to God “the Father,” whom he referred to in 15:24. Use a translation that clearly refers to God the Son.
Here, himself focuses attention on the Son and emphasizes that the Son is the one doing this.
Here, just as in 15:27, the Corinthians would have known that the one having subjected all things is God the Father.
Here, God could refer to: (1) God the Father specifically; (2) all three persons that are God.
Here, all in all is a phrase that emphasizes that God rules and controls everything that exists.
15:29: τί ποιήσουσιν, οἱ βαπτιζόμενοι ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν
Paul does not ask this question because he is looking for information. Rather, he asks it to involve the Corinthians in what he is arguing.
ποιήσουσιν, οἱ βαπτιζόμενοι ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν

Here Paul speaks of “doing” something in the future. He could be referring to: (1) the intended result of being baptized, which happens after the baptism; (2) what the people being baptized think that they are doing.

It is unclear what being baptized for the dead actually means and what kind of practice it refers to. What is clear is that the practice only makes sense if one believes that the dead are raised. If possible, express these phrases in general terms. Two of the most common ways to understand being baptized for the dead are that it could refer to: (1) the practice of living believers receiving baptism in place of people who died without being baptized; (2) people receiving baptism because they believe that the dead will “rise.” They could be expecting their own resurrection or the resurrection of people they knew who are dead.
Paul does not ask this question because he is looking for information. Rather, he asks it to involve the Corinthians in what he is arguing.
15:30: τί καὶ ἡμεῖς κινδυνεύομεν πᾶσαν ὥραν
Paul does not ask this question because he is looking for information. Rather, he asks it to involve the Corinthians in what he is arguing.
Here Paul says that we are in danger because of the work that he and others do to proclaim the gospel.
Here, every hour identifies an action as frequent or consistent. It does not mean that Paul and others experienced danger once every hour.
15:31: Here Paul speaks as if he “dies” every day. Paul does not experience death every single day, but he speaks in this way to emphasize that he could die at many different times. He speaks in this way to emphasize how often he experiences danger and risks losing his life.
The phrase by the is an oath formula. Here, by introduces a person or thing that a person swears by to prove the truth of a claim.
ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, τῷ Κυρίῳ ἡμῶν

Here Paul uses the spatial metaphor in Christ Jesus our Lord to describe the union of believers with Christ. In this case, being in Christ, or united to Christ, identifies Paul’s boasting as something that only matters or is valid in his union with Christ.
15:32: Paul does not ask this question because he is looking for information. Rather, he asks it to involve the Corinthians in what he is arguing.
Here, the profit to me refers to something that is good for Paul.
Here, according to men identifies thinking or acting in only human ways.

Here, the wild beasts could be: (1) a figurative reference to enemies, who acted like wild beasts. In support of this is the fact that, except for this verse, the Bible does not talk about Paul fighting wild beasts; (2) a literal reference to fighting wild animals.

Ephesus was a city on the west coast of what is now Turkey. Paul spent time there soon after leaving Corinth (See: Acts 18:19–21). After some more travels, he visited Ephesus and stayed there for more than two years (Acts 19:1–20:1). Neither story mentions wild beasts, and Paul does not clarify which visit he is speaking about.
Here, Let us eat and drink refers to lavish or wild eating and drinking. It does not refer to regular meals.
Here, tomorrow refers to a time that will come soon. It does not necessarily refer to the day after today. The saying uses tomorrow to emphasize how soon we will die.
15:33: In Paul’s culture, this statement was a proverb that many people would have been familiar with. The proverb means that bad friends turn a good person into a bad person.
Here, Bad company refers to a persons’ friends who normally do what is wrong.
Here, good morals refers to the character of a person who habitually does what is good or right.
15:34: Here, Be sober refers to someone becoming sober after they were drunk. Paul speaks in this way to characterize how the Corinthians are acting and thinking as if they were drunk. He wants them to no longer act as if they are in a stupor or asleep and instead be alert and in their right mind.
Here, I say this to your shame is Paul’s way of telling the Corinthians that they should feel ashamed about how some of them have no knowledge of God.
15:35: Here, the person asking the question speaks as if the dead can come. This could refer to: (1) the existence of the dead. In other words, come would refer to anything that the dead do; (2) how the believing dead come with Christ when he returns to earth.
15:36: ὃ σπείρεις, οὐ ζῳοποιεῖται, ἐὰν μὴ ἀποθάνῃ
In 15:36–38, Paul speaks about how farmers sow seeds as an analogy for understanding how the dead resurrect.
ὃ σπείρεις, οὐ ζῳοποιεῖται, ἐὰν μὴ ἀποθάνῃ

Here Paul speaks about farming practices that were common in his culture. A farmer would sow seeds on the dirt in a field, and the seed would sink into the field and seemingly “die.” Only after a period where it lies “dead” in the ground does the seed live in new form as a plant. Paul specifically uses live and die to connect the farming practices to human life and death, so if possible use terms that can apply to both humans and seeds.
15:37: Paul continues to use an analogy from farming. In this verse, he focuses on how the living plant that grows from a seed looks nothing like that seed.

Here, the body that will be identifies the plant that will later grow from the seed. Paul’s point is that one does not sow something that looks like the fully grown plant. Rather, one sows a bare seed.
Here, a bare seed refers to a seed all by itself, with no leaves or stem like the plant will later have.
εἰ τύχοι σίτου, ἤ τινος τῶν λοιπῶν

Here Paul uses wheat as an example of a plant that was common in culture and that starts out as a seed. When he says or something else, he makes it clear that any kind of plant that begins as a seed works for his analogy.
15:38: Here Paul concludes his analogy about farming. In the last verse he proved that seeds grow into bodies that look nothing like the seeds. Here, he shows that God is one who decides what body a seed grows into and God gives different kinds of “bodies” to different kinds of seeds. Again, the main verbal connection between human resurrection and seeds growing is the word body, so if possible use a word for body that can apply to both seeds and humans.
Here, just as he desires means that God has chosen what kind of body every seed will grow into, and he does this as he thinks best.
Here, each of the seeds could refer to: (1) each of the varieties or kinds of seeds that exist; (2) each individual seed.
15:39: Paul repeats flesh of and the same structure in four consecutive clauses. This was worded powerfully in his culture, and it emphasizes the distinctions between the different kinds of flesh.
Here, animals refers to living things that are not men, birds, or fish but still count as animals. The word often refers particularly to domesticated animals such as sheep, goats, oxen, or horses.
15:40: Here, heavenly bodies refers to the kinds of things that Paul will mention in the next verse: the sun, moon, and stars (15:41). The earthly bodies are the kinds of things Paul mentioned in the previous verse: humans, animals, birds, and fish (15:39).
Here Paul is distinguishing between different kinds of glory.
15:41: Here, just as in 15:40, Paul is distinguishing between different kinds of glory.
Paul repeats glory of and the same structure in three consecutive clauses. This was worded powerfully in his culture, and it emphasizes the distinctions between the different kinds of glory.
15:42: Here Paul speaks as if a dead body were sown like a seed. He speaks in this way to connect how a dead body is buried in the ground with how a seed is sown in the ground. However, Paul does not continue the metaphor when he talks about how the body is raised, since those are his normal words for speaking about resurrection.
15:43: Here Paul repeats is sown in, is raised in, and similar structure in three consecutive sentences (See: the end of 15:42). This was worded powerfully in his culture, and it emphasizes the three distinctions between how the body is sown and raised.
σπείρεται ἐν ἀτιμίᾳ … σπείρεται ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ

Here, just as in 15:42, Paul speaks as if a dead body were sown like a seed. He speaks in this way to connect how a dead body is buried in the ground to how a seed is sown in the ground. However, Paul does not continue the metaphor when he talks about how the body is raised, since those are his normal words for speaking about resurrection.
15:44: Here, just as in 15:42–43, Paul speaks as if a dead body were sown like a seed. He speaks in this way to connect how a dead body is buried in the ground with how a seed is sown in the ground. However, Paul does not continue the metaphor when he talks about how the body is raised, since those are his normal words for speaking about resurrection.
Here, natural body refers to human bodies before they are raised. These bodies are those that function in the ways that we can observe right now and that fit with life on earth right now.

Here, spiritual {body} refers to human bodies after they are raised. It could specifically refer to: (1) how the body is controlled by God’s Spirit and thus fits with how people will live when God renews everything he has created; (2) how the {body} is made out of spirit as opposed to soul or flesh.
15:45: Here, soul is a different form of the word that was translated as “natural” in 15:44. Paul uses this similar word to make the point that Adam had a “natural body” when God created him.

Here, The last Adam refers to Jesus. Paul wishes to draw connections between Adam and Jesus, and so he calls Adam the first man Adam, and he calls Jesus the last Adam. Each “Adam” is the first person to have a specific kind of body: the first Adam has a “natural body” as a living soul, while the last Adam has a “spiritual body” as a life-giving spirit.
Here, spirit is a different form of the word that was translated as “spiritual” in 15:44. Paul uses this similar word to make the point that Jesus had a “spiritual body” after his resurrection.
Here, life-giving refers to how Jesus, The last Adam, “gives” the “life” that he now has to everyone who believes in him.
15:46: Here, just as in 15:44, spiritual refers to human bodies after they are raised. It could specifically refer to: (1) how the body is controlled by God’s Spirit and thus fits with how people will live when God renews everything he has created; (2) how the body is made out of “spirit” as opposed to “soul” or “flesh.”

Here, just as in 15:44, natural refers to human bodies before they are raised. These bodies are those that function in the ways that we can observe right now and that fit with life on earth right now.
15:47: ὁ πρῶτος ἄνθρωπος … ὁ δεύτερος ἄνθρωπος

Here, first man refers to Adam, the first human whom God created. The second man refers to Jesus, the first human to receive the new resurrection body. Paul describes them as first and second because Adam was the first to receive a specific kind of body, and Jesus was the second to receive a specific kind of body, a body different than the body that Adam received. This is the same point he made in the last verse about which body comes “first” (15:46).

Here Paul refers again to Genesis 2:7. In that verse, we learn about how God made the first man, Adam, out of dust. Paul uses this reference to dust to prove that the first man has the kind of life and body that belongs on the earth. So, of the earth means almost the same thing that “natural” means in 15:46.

Here, from heaven could refer to: (1) how Jesus, the second man, has a body and life fit for heaven and the new creation. In this case, from heaven would mean basically the same thing that “spiritual” means in 15:46; (2) how Jesus, the second man, came from heaven when he became a human.
15:48: Here, the ones of earth refers to people who are not united to Jesus and who thus belong to the earth. Paul uses this language to connect these people with the earthly first man.
Here, the ones of heaven refers to people who are united to Jesus and who thus belong to heaven, as Jesus does. Paul uses this language to connect these people with the heavenly second man.
15:49: Here, to bear the image of something or somebody refers to being similar to that thing or person.

Here Paul does not specify whose bodies the earthly and the heavenly refer to. However, the previous verses imply that the earthly body belongs to the “first man,” Adam, while the heavenly body belongs to the “second man,” Jesus.
In Paul’s language, let us also bear and “we will also bear” look and sound very similar. Both options have some evidence to support them.
15:50: Here Paul makes two very similar statements in which flesh and blood goes with perishable and the kingdom of God goes with imperishable. These two statements could: (1) be basically synonymous, and Paul repeats himself to emphasize the point.
This phrase expresses a single idea by using two words connected with and. The words flesh and blood together describe the human body as it currently exists.
Here, flesh and blood represents a body that is made out of flesh and blood.

Here Paul speaks of the kingdom of God that is imperishable as if it were property that a parent could pass on to their child when the parent dies. He speaks in this way to indicate that believers will eventually receive and live in the3 kingdom of God that God has promised to them.
Here, perishable and imperishable identify whether people or things last or fall apart. These words are the same ones translated as “decay” and “immortality” in 15:42.
15:51: Here Paul refers to how people die as if they fall asleep. This is a polite way of referring to something unpleasant.
15:52: Here, instant refers to the smallest segment of time that Paul and the Corinthians knew about. He means that the “change” (15:51) will happen so quickly that it will only take up the smallest bit of time.

Here, in the twinkling of an eye refers to the speed at which one moves or blinks one’s eye. Paul’s point is that the “change” (15:51) will take place so quickly that one cannot move one’s eye fast enough to see it, or if one blinks, one might miss it.
ἐν τῇ ἐσχάτῃ σάλπιγγι; σαλπίσει γάρ

Paul refers briefly to the last trumpet without explanation because the Corinthians would have known what he was talking about. In Paul’s culture, people knew that a trumpet would sound to signal the Day of the Lord, in this case, the day when Jesus comes back, the dead rise, and the world is renewed. An angel or archangel would blow this trumpet.
Here, imperishable identifies people or things that last and do not fall apart. See you how translated this word in 15:50.
15:53: Here Paul makes two very similar statements in which perishable goes with mortal and incorruptibility goes with immortality. These two statements are basically synonymous, and Paul repeats himself to emphasize the point.
Here, perishable and incorruptibility identify whether people or things last or fall apart.

Here Paul speaks as if the perishable and the mortal could put on incorruptibility and immortality like they were pieces of clothing. He does not mean that believers still have what is perishable and mortal somehow underneath incorruptibility and immortality. Instead, Paul uses the metaphor to illustrate how people will change identity from what is perishable and mortal to incorruptibility and immortality.
Here, mortal and immortality identify whether people or things die or cannot die.
15:54: Here, these clauses repeat the words found at the end of the last verse (15:53). Paul repeats these words to make what he is arguing very clear.

Here Paul makes two very similar statements in which perishable goes with mortal and incorruptibility goes with immortality. These two statements are basically synonymous, and Paul repeats himself to emphasize the point.

Here, mortal and immortality identify whether people or things die or cannot die.
Here, will come about identifies that something will happen or come to pass.
Here, word represents what someone says or writes in words.
Here the quote refers to Death as if it were food that could be swallowed up. This illustrates that Death has been defeated as surely as if someone devoured it as though death were food.
15:55: Here Paul quotes how Hosea addresses something that he knows cannot hear him, Death, in order to show his listeners in a strong way how he feels about it.
Paul quotes how Hosea repeats O death, where {is} your. Parallel structures like this were poetic in Hosea’s culture.

Paul does not quote these questions because he is looking for information about where death’s victory and sting are. Rather, the questions involve the Corinthians in what Paul is arguing. The question assumes that the answer is “nowhere.” In other words, there is no victory or sting for Death.
Both appearances of your refer back to Death and are singular.

Here, sting refers to a sharp point, particularly the kind that insects have that can pierce skin, inject poison, and cause pain. The author of this quotation (Hosea) speaks as if Death has a sting, referring to how death causes pain both for the person who dies and for others who have lost someone they love.
15:56: τὸ … κέντρον τοῦ θανάτου ἡ ἁμαρτία
Here, the sting of death refers back to the same words in the quote in 15:56.
15:57: Here, thanks {be} to God is a way to indicate that one is praising God for something.
Here Paul does not express whom the victory is over.
15:58: Here, both steadfast and immovable refer to people who hold their positions steadily. The word steadfast emphasizes that someone is reliable or faithful, while immovable emphasizes that someone is stable and cannot be moved. Paul uses two similar words to emphasize the need to maintain one position.

Here Paul speaks as if he wanted the Corinthians to be an object or thing that stays in one place. He speaks in this way because he wants them to continue to believe the gospel as firmly as if it was a location that they could remain in.
Here, in vain identifies a cause that does not have its intended effect. In this case, the Corinthians’ labor is not in vain because it is in the Lord and will thus lead to its intended effect.

Here Paul uses the spatial metaphor in the Lord to describe the union of believers with the Lord. In this case, being in the Lord or united to the Lord identifies why the Corinthians can “know” that their labor is not in vain.
16:1: Here, the collection refers to money that is “collected” from people for a specific purpose. Here Paul clarifies that it is “collected” for the saints.

Here Paul does not clarify which saints he is speaking about. However, in 16:3, he states that this collection will be taken to “Jerusalem.” Therefore, the saints are Jewish people who believe in Jesus.
16:2: Here, the first of the week refers to the first day of the week in the Jewish calendar, which is the day we call Sunday. It is also the day on which Christians would hold special gatherings since Jesus rose from the dead on this day of the week.
Here Paul uses a third-person imperative.
Here, to put {something} aside refers to putting some money in a specific location in one’s house to use later for a specific purpose.
Here, storing up refers to saving something, which in this case is money. Use a word or phrase that refers to saving money.

Here, whatever he might have prospered refers to how much money a person earned. Here, the phrase could specifically refer to: (1) how much more a person made than what they needed or expected. Paul would thus be asking the Corinthians to put {something} aside from the extra money that they received; (2) the amount a person made in a specific period of time. Paul would thus be asking the Corinthians to put {something} aside in proportion to how much they made during a week.
Here, collections refers to “collecting” money from people for a specific purpose.
16:3: Here, those whom the Corinthians approve are those whom they consider to be trustworthy and able to accomplish the task of taking the money to Jerusalem.

In Paul’s culture, messengers and travelers often carried a letter or letters that were meant to introduce them to the person they were going to visit. These kinds of letters usually stated that the messenger or traveler was trustworthy and should be welcomed. Here, the letters could be from: (1) Paul; (2) the Corinthians.
16:4: Here, appropriate identifies an action that fits or matches the situation. Paul does not explicitly state who thinks it is appropriate. It could be: (1) both Paul and the Corinthians; (2) just Paul.
16:6: Here, perhaps indicates that Paul is uncertain about how long he will stay with the Corinthians.
Here, to help people on their way refers to assisting them with the things that they need to travel, including food and money.

Here, wherever I might go identifies the place Paul will visit after he visits the Corinthians, but it does not state where that place is. In other words, Paul will travel somewhere else, but he does not say where.
16:7: Here, to see people refers to spending time with them, not just seeing them.
Here, only in passing refers to a brief time, particularly a time between two other events. Paul is referring to a short visit while traveling somewhere else.
Here, for some time refers to a longer period of time than only in passing.
Here, if the Lord would permit means that Paul plans on traveling in the ways he has described, but he acknowledges that this will only happen if that is what the Lord allows him to do.
16:9: θύρα … μοι ἀνέῳγεν μεγάλη καὶ ἐνεργής

Paul speaks of his opportunity to preach the gospel in Ephesus as if someone had opened a door for him to enter into a room. He describes this door as wide to indicate that the opportunity is great. He describes the door as effective to indicate that his work is producing results.
Here Paul speaks as if the door opens itself, but he implies that “God” is the one who has opened the door.
16:10: Here, see that refers to carefully doing something or making sure that something happens.
Here Paul implies that the Corinthians could make Timothy “afraid.” Throughout the letter, it has been clear that some of the Corinthians disagree with and even oppose Paul.
16:11: Here Paul uses a third-person imperative.
Here, despise refers to how people treat others who have low status, including looking down on them and ignoring them.
Here, just as in 16:6, to help people on their way refers to assisting them with the things that they need to travel, including food and money.
Here Paul is expecting Timothy to travel back to where Paul is.
Here, the brothers could be: (1) traveling with Timothy, and Paul is expecting their return along with Timothy; (2) with Paul, expecting Timothy to return.
16:12: Here, brother identifies Apollos as a fellow believer. Apollos was male, although brother does not emphasize this.
Here, not at all makes a stronger negation than not by itself. Use a word or phrase that makes a negation stronger.

Here, to have the opportunity refers to when the situation is right or appropriate for some action. Most likely, Paul means that Apollos will visit the Corinthians when he has time and when he thinks it is the proper time to do so.
16:13: Here, Stay alert refers to keeping oneself from falling asleep.

Here Paul speaks as if the faith were something solid in which the Corinthians could stand firm. He speaks in this way because he wants them to persevere in the faith as much as people stand firm on the ground. People trust the ground to hold them up, and they can stand on it for a long time. In the same way, Paul wants the Corinthians to trust and persevere in the faith.
Here, act like men is a way to urge someone to be brave and courageous. The opposite of acting like men is acting like cowards.
Here, be strong does not refer to physical strength but rather to mental strength or determination.
16:14: Here Paul uses a third-person imperative.
Here, all your things refers to everything that a person thinks and does.
16:15: Stephanas is the name of a man. Paul already mentioned his household in 1:16.

Here, firstfruits refers to what farmers first gathered from their fields. Often, these firstfruits were offered to God to thank him for providing food. What Paul emphasizes here is that firstfruits are the first products from a field, although the word also implies that there will be more products.
Achaia is the name of a province in the southern part of what we call Greece. The city of Corinth is in this province.
Here, they have devoted themselves refers to how these people decided to spend most of their time doing something specific.
16:16: Here, joining together in the work and laboring mean very similar things. The phrase joining together in the work emphasizes that people are working together. The word laboring emphasizes that the people are working hard.
16:17: Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus are the names of three men. Stephanas is the same man whom Paul mentioned in 16:15.
Here, supplied refers to filling something up or making something complete. Here Paul says that these three men supplied, or filled up or completed, whatever Paul and the Corinthians were lacking.

This could refer to: (1) what Paul is lacking in his relationship with the Corinthians. In other words, Paul misses the Corinthians and wishes he was with them; (2) what the Corinthians are lacking in how they are helping Paul. In other words, the Corinthians were not helping Paul very much until these three men arrived.
16:18: ἀνέπαυσαν … τὸ ἐμὸν πνεῦμα καὶ τὸ ὑμῶν

Here, refreshed my spirit and yours refers to how these three men helped Paul and the Corinthians regain energy, strength, and confidence. In other words, they helped Paul and the Corinthians feel better and stronger.
τὸ ἐμὸν πνεῦμα καὶ τὸ ὑμῶν
Here, spirit is part of the idiom “refresh the spirit.”Paul assumes that his readers will understand that it refers to the spirit of the person, or their inner life, not to the Holy Spirit.
16:19: As was customary in his culture, Paul concludes the letter by extending greetings from people who are with him and who know the people to whom he is writing.

Here, enthusiastically indicates that Aquila and Priscilla wish to greet the Corinthians especially strongly or with extra friendship. Use a word or phrase that identifies an especially strong or friendly greeting.

Here Paul uses the spatial metaphor in the Lord to describe the union of believers with Christ. In this case, being in the Lord, or united to the Lord, identifies the greeting from Aquila and Priscilla as something that they give because both they and the Corinthians are united to the Lord.
16:20: Here, All the brothers refers to fellow believers. They could be: (1) everyone in Ephesus (where Paul is) who wishes to say hello to the believers in Corinth; (2) the believers who travel and work with Paul.
Here Paul continues to extend greetings from people who are with him.
Since this letter would be read in public to the Corinthian believers, Paul wishes them to Greet each other in this situation. If possible, translate Greet as you did earlier in the verse.

Here, a holy kiss describes a kiss that believers would give to other believers (that is why it is holy). In Paul’s culture, this was an appropriate way to greet someone with whom one was very close, such as a family member or a good friend.
16:21: Paul concludes his letter by writing a final greeting to the Corinthians.

In Paul’s culture, it was normal for a scribe to write down what the author of the letter was saying. Paul here indicates that he himself is writing these last words. He may mean just this verse, or he may mean the rest of the letter. The phrase in my own hand means that it was Paul’s “own hand” that took up the pen and wrote.
16:22: Here Paul uses a third-person imperative.
This is an Aramaic word. Paul spelled it out using Greek letters so his readers would know how it sounded.
16:23: ἡ χάρις τοῦ Κυρίου Ἰησοῦ μεθ’ ὑμῶν
As was customary in his culture, Paul closes his letter with a blessing for the Corinthians.
16:24: Here Paul uses the spatial metaphor in Christ Jesus to describe the union of believers with Christ. In this case, being in Christ Jesus, or united to Christ, identifies Paul’s love as something that he does because both he and the Corinthians are united to Christ.
Many early manuscripts include Amen here. However some early manuscripts do not include it, and it is possible that scribes added it because some letters end with Amen.
